title: 1 Kings 5:13–18
context: 1 Kings 5:13–18 describes the labor force for the temple. Versification: English 5:13–18 is Hebrew 5:27–32; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men from Israel, who work in Lebanon in monthly shifts under Adoniram, along with large numbers of burden bearers, stonecutters, and overseers. Costly foundation stones are cut and prepared by Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders, and the Gebalites. Interpreters note the tension between this levy and 1 Kings 9:22, which says Solomon did not make Israelites slaves, and the later resentment of forced labor (1 Kings 12:4, 18). Both traditions read the passage as honest history that records the temple’s glory alongside its human cost.

verses.text: King Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men from all Israel. Arminian readers note the heavy demand on the people and many connect it with Samuel’s warning that a king would take their sons for his work (1 Samuel 8:11–17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the levy foreshadows later burdens. Interpreters discuss how it fits with 1 Kings 9:22, which says Israelites were not made slaves, and many distinguish rotating labor service from permanent slavery. Both traditions treat the question without forcing a resolution.

verses.text: He sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand a month by courses: for a month they were in Lebanon, and two months at home; and Adoniram was over the men subject to forced labor.
verses.arminianNotes: The workers go to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, one month there and two months home, under Adoniram. Arminians see some care for the workers in the rotation, which allowed time with their families and their own work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that Adoniram is probably the same Adoram later stoned by Israel during the revolt against Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:18). Both traditions see the verse as part of a frank record of the cost of the temple and of later resentment.

verses.text: Solomon had seventy thousand who bore burdens, and eighty thousand who were stone cutters in the mountains,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon has seventy thousand burden bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters in the hills. Arminian readers see the massive scale of the labor force, which shows both the grandeur of the project and the weight it placed on the population.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Interpreters note that 2 Chronicles 2:17–18 describes these workers as foreigners living in Israel. Both traditions read the numbers as showing the size of the work without building doctrine on them.

verses.text: besides Solomon’s chief officers who were over the work: three thousand three hundred who ruled over the people who labored in the work.
verses.arminianNotes: There are also three thousand three hundred chief officers over the work. Arminians see careful organization of a large project, with Solomon’s administrative wisdom on display in the way the work is supervised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that 2 Chronicles 2:18 gives a somewhat different figure for the overseers. Both traditions treat the difference as a question of counting categories and avoid making it a theological issue.

verses.text: The king commanded, and they cut out large stones, costly stones, to lay the foundation of the house with worked stone.
verses.arminianNotes: At the king’s command, large and costly stones are cut to lay the foundation with worked stone. Arminian readers see the best materials given for God’s house, a sign of the honor due to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the foundation stones were hidden once the building stood, yet they were still costly. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the work for God’s house was done with care even where it would not be seen.

verses.text: Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders and the Gebalites cut them, and prepared the timber and the stones to build the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders, and the Gebalites cut the stones and prepare timber and stone for the house. Arminians see Israelites and foreigners working side by side, which shows that the LORD’s house was built with help from beyond Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The Gebalites are usually identified as people of Gebal, the Phoenician city later called Byblos. Both traditions see God using the skills of many peoples for his house, which some connect with later prophetic hopes for the nations.
